Chapter 5: Restoring Trust When It Has Been Broken
Even when we do our best, sometimes trust gets broken. Maybe it’s a simple mistake, a promise that wasn’t kept, or just a misunderstanding that spiraled out of control. But here’s some good news—trust might be fragile, but it’s also surprisingly resilient. If you approach it the right way, you can often rebuild trust... and sometimes, it ends up even stronger than it was before.
So, how do you actually restore trust when it’s taken a hit? Well, it all starts with one crucial step: acknowledging what happened. This means facing the issue head-on, not dodging it or making excuses. People need to hear you admit what went wrong, and understand how it affected them. If you try to sweep things under the rug, or downplay the problem, you only make the wound deeper.
Next, it’s all about responsibility. You’ve got to own your part in what happened—no finger-pointing, no shifting blame. And when you apologize, make sure it’s real. A sincere, specific apology carries a lot of weight. It shows you’re not just sorry things turned out this way, but you genuinely understand the impact.
But don’t stop there. Making amends is where your actions start to line up with your words. Maybe you fix the mistake, offer to make things right, or set up new habits to make sure it won’t happen again. The main thing? Show, don’t just tell, that things will be different from now on.
Here’s another thing to keep in mind—restoring trust takes patience. People need time to see that your changes are sticking. It’s the small, consistent actions over time that really rebuild what was lost. Every time you follow through on a new promise, you’re adding back into that “trust account.”
So, what are some practical steps you can take if you’re working to rebuild trust? Let’s break it down:
First, admit the mistake openly and take full responsibility.
Second, apologize sincerely, focusing on how it affected the other person—not just your intentions.
Third, make concrete changes to fix the root of the problem.
Fourth, keep communicating, share your progress, and ask for feedback.
And finally, be patient and persistent. Trust takes time to rebuild, so hang in there.
Of course, not every breach of trust is the same. Some issues are pretty minor and can be fixed quickly. Others go deeper, and might take longer—or might never fully heal. But even when it’s tough, trying to restore trust shows real integrity and respect for the relationship.
If you’re a leader, this is especially important. When leaders admit mistakes and work hard to make things right, they set the tone for everyone else. It creates a culture where honesty and accountability are just part of how things work.
At the end of the day, restoring trust isn’t just about patching up what went wrong. It’s a chance to make relationships even stronger, and to really understand each other better. Sometimes, working through a breach can actually lead to more empathy, learning, and genuine connection.
So if you ever find yourself needing to rebuild trust, remember—it’s absolutely possible. With openness, responsibility, and patience, you can turn a setback into a new beginning.
